section.content: Training of machine learning algorithms using interpretable artificial intelligence. Training of a machine learning algorithm (111) is performed. A machine learning algorithm (111) performs a classification prediction (115) based on feature vectors (101) representing the radar measurement data set. The weights considered in the training are determined using interpretable artificial intelligence analysis.
使用可解释人工智能对机器学习算法的训练。执行机器学习算法(111)的训练。机器学习算法(111)基于表示雷达测量数据集的特征向量(101)进行分类预测(115)。训练中考虑的权重是使用可解释人工智能分析来确定的。

Training of machine learning algorithms using interpretable artificial intelligenceTechnical Field

Various examples of the present disclosure generally relate to classification predictions based on radar measurement datasets using machine learning algorithms. The various examples relate specifically to aspects of training of machine learning algorithms.

Background

Machine Learning (ML) algorithms are widely used for making predictions. For example, the hidden observable of a measurement may be revealed by processing the corresponding measurement dataset. One particular area of application for ML algorithms is in making predictions based on radar measurement data sets acquired using radar measurements. For example, classification predictions, such as classification predictions for demographics or gesture classification, may be implemented using ML algorithms.

Examples are disclosed herein: santra, A., hazra, S. (2020) Deep Learning Applications of Short-Range radars.United Kingdom: artech House.

Disclosure of Invention

There is a need for a technique that facilitates accurate predictions using ML algorithms, particularly based on radar measurement datasets.

This need is met by the features of the independent claims. The features of the dependent claims define embodiments.

It is to be understood that the features mentioned above and those yet to be explained below can be used not only in the respective combinations indicated, but also in other combinations or alone, without departing from the scope of the present invention.

Detailed Description

Some examples of the present disclosure generally provide a plurality of circuits or other electrical devices. All references to circuits and other electrical devices and functions provided by each are not intended to be limited to inclusion of only what is shown and described herein. While certain tags may be assigned to the various circuits or other electrical devices disclosed, such tags are not intended to limit the scope of operation of the circuits and other electrical devices. Such circuits and other electrical devices may be combined with and/or separated from each other in any manner based on the particular type of electrical implementation desired. It should be appreciated that any of the circuits or other electrical devices disclosed herein may include any number of microcontrollers, graphics Processor Units (GPUs), integrated circuits, memory devices (e.g., flash memory, random Access Memory (RAM), read Only Memory (ROM), electrically Programmable Read Only Memory (EPROM), electrically Erasable Programmable Read Only Memory (EEPROM), or other suitable variations thereof), and software that cooperate with each other to perform the operations disclosed herein. Furthermore, any one or more of the electrical devices can be configured to execute program code embodied in a non-transitory computer readable medium programmed to perform any number of the disclosed functions.

Hereinafter, examples of the present disclosure will be described in detail with reference to the accompanying drawings. It should be understood that the following description of examples should not be taken in a limiting sense. The scope of the present disclosure is not intended to be limited by the examples or figures described below, which are to be considered illustrative only.

The figures should not be taken as schematic representations and the elements shown in the figures are not necessarily shown to scale. Rather, the various elements are represented such that their function and general purpose will be apparent to those skilled in the art. Any connection or coupling between functional blocks, devices, components, or other physical or functional units shown in the figures or described herein may also be achieved by indirect connection or coupling. The coupling between the components may also be established through a wireless connection. The functional blocks may be implemented in hardware, firmware, software, or a combination thereof.

Various examples of the present disclosure generally relate to using ML algorithms to solve classification tasks based on radar measurements.

Various classification tasks are conceivable. Examples include people counting. Here, determining the number of people in the scene; different candidate classes are associated with different people. Another example involves motion classification. The disclosed techniques may be used to identify and classify various types of motion. For example, a gesture class of a gesture performed by the object may be determined. Different candidate classes relate to different gestures. Other examples of motion classification will relate to kicking motion classification. An intelligent trunk opener is a concept of opening and closing a trunk or a door of a vehicle without using an automatic and handsfree key. The kick-off action is performed by the user using the foot.

Various techniques disclosed herein employ radar measurements of a scene including one or more objects (e.g., a hand or finger or hand-held object (such as a stylus or beacon), or one or more persons) to obtain data based on which classification predictions may be made. For example, short range radar measurements may be implemented. Here, the radar chirp may be used to measure the position of one or more objects in a scene having a range of tens of centimeters or meters.

According to various examples disclosed herein, millimeter wave radar sensors may be used to perform radar measurements; the radar sensor operates as a Frequency Modulated Continuous Wave (FMCW) radar that includes millimeter wave radar sensor circuitry, one or more transmitters, and one or more receivers. Millimeter wave radar sensors may transmit and receive signals in the range of 20GHz to 122 GHz. Alternatively, frequencies outside this range may be used, such as frequencies between 1GHz and 20GHz, or frequencies between 122GHz and 300 GHz.

The radar sensor may transmit a plurality of radar pulses, such as chirp, to the scene. This refers to pulsed operation. In some embodiments, the chirp is a linear chirp, i.e., the instantaneous frequency of the chirp varies linearly with time.

The doppler shift may be used to determine the velocity of the target. Thus, the measurement data provided by the radar sensor may indicate depth positions of a plurality of objects of the scene. The speed may also be indicated.

The radar sensor may output a measurement frame. In general, a measurement frame (sometimes also referred to as a data frame or physical frame) includes data samples of a plurality of radar pulses (particularly chirps) within a particular sampling time. The slow time increases with the chirp; the fast time is incremented for subsequent samples. Channel dimensions for different antennas may be used. The radar sensor outputs a time series of measurement frames.

Compared to camera-based gesture classification, radar measurement-based gesture classification has the following advantages: the lighting conditions are unchanged; privacy is protected; subtle gesture actions can be captured.

According to various examples, ML algorithms are used to make classification predictions based on radar measurement datasets.

An example implementation of the ML algorithm is a neural network algorithm (hereinafter simply referred to as neural network NN). An NN generally includes a plurality of nodes that may be arranged in a plurality of layers. The nodes of a given layer are connected to one or more nodes of a subsequent layer. A jump connection between non-adjacent layers is also possible. Typically, the connections are also referred to as edges. The output of each node may be calculated based on the value of each of one or more nodes connected to the input. Nonlinear calculations are possible. Different layers may perform different transformations, e.g., pooling, max pooling, weighted or unweighted summation, nonlinear activation, convolution, etc. The NN may include a plurality of hidden layers disposed between an input layer and an output layer. One example NN is a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). Here, one-dimensional (1-D) or two-dimensional (2-D) convolution layers are used, as well as other layers. For classification prediction, a Softmax classification layer may be used at the output of NN. Here, the softmax function is used, and cross entropy loss is typically used during training.

The computation performed by the node is set by the corresponding weight associated with the node. The weights may be determined in training of NN (details will be described in connection with blocks 3115 and 3215). For this purpose, numerical optimization may be used to set the weights. A penalty function may be defined between the output of the NN and the desired reference truth label (ground truth label), which is required to be minimized during training (details will be described in connection with fig. 9). For this purpose, a gradient descent technique may be employed, wherein the weights are adjusted from the rear to the front of the NN.

According to various examples, the ML algorithm may consider different inputs. The type of input data may vary with the type of ML algorithm; which may vary with the type of classification prediction by the ML algorithm. Nonetheless, in the following, some examples of potential input data are disclosed. According to various examples, a range-doppler image (RDI) may be provided as an input to the ML algorithm. Doppler domain filtering may be applied to produce micro-motion and macro-motion RDI; one or both of which may be used as inputs to the ML algorithm. For example, a Fourier Transform (FT) may be performed on the radar measurement data for each measurement frame along the fast time dimension to obtain RDI. According to other examples, a range elevation image along with a range azimuth image may be provided as an input to the ML algorithm, i.e., a 2-D angle map. In some examples, the ML algorithm may make the classification prediction based on one or more one-dimensional (1-D) time series of respective observables of radar measurements associated with the object.

Various examples are based on the following findings: that is, since the ML algorithm is a nature of a black box, it is often difficult to explain why the ML algorithm makes a correct or incorrect classification prediction.

To address this problem, interpretable artificial intelligence (XAI) analysis can be used to interpret and find weaknesses of the ML algorithm. XAI analysis can be used to configure the training process. This helps to improve the accuracy of the ML algorithm.

Further, various examples are based on the following findings: that is, the available training data sets typically have a finite size. The accuracy of the ML algorithm may be limited due to the limited amount of training data available. In this case, this will result in a significant increase in the error rate of the classification predictions.

To alleviate these limitations, according to various examples, the training data set may be enhanced. That is, based on the available training data, additional training data may be generated. Different options may be used to generate additional training data. For example, the enhanced training data set may be derived from the initial training data set. In particular, one or more data operations may be applied to training feature vectors of an initial training data set to obtain enhanced training feature vectors of an enhanced training data set. Furthermore, joint learning techniques may also be employed. Here, an additional set of joint training data may be acquired that includes observations of previously invisible scenes of the deployed sensors. This also helps to improve the accuracy of the ML algorithm.

Further, various examples are based on the following findings: that is, sometimes retraining the ML algorithm with additional training data can lead to a "forget" situation. Here, the prediction accuracy may deteriorate due to retraining of the ML algorithm; this is because weights that have been trained in an early training round may be covered, at least to some extent, by a new training round (overwrite). To alleviate this, incremental learning is employed. Here, to retrain the ML algorithm, the early training dataset and the subsequent training dataset are jointly considered.

Fig. 1 schematically illustrates a system 65. The system 65 includes a radar sensor 70 and a processing device 60. The processing device 60 may obtain measurement data 64 from the radar sensor 70. For example, the processing device may be an embedded device, a smart phone, a smart watch, or the like.

A processor 62, such as a general purpose processor (central processing unit CPU), field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA), application Specific Integrated Circuit (ASIC), may receive the measurement data 64 via the interface 61 and process the measurement data 64. For example, the measurement data 64 may include a time series of measurement frames, each measurement frame including a sample of an ADC converter.

Processor 62 may load program code from memory 63 and execute the program code. The processor 62 may then perform techniques as disclosed herein, e.g., processing the input data using an ML algorithm, classifying predictions using an ML algorithm, training an ML algorithm, and so forth.

Details regarding such processing will be explained in more detail below; however, first, details concerning the radar sensor 70 will be explained.

Fig. 2 shows aspects related to the radar sensor 70. The radar sensor 70 includes a processor 72 (labeled as a digital signal processor DSP) coupled to a memory 73. Based on program code stored in memory 73, processor 72 may perform various functions related to transmitting radar pulses 86 using transmit antenna 77 and digital-to-analog converter (DAC) 75. Once the radar pulse 86 has been reflected by the scene 80, the processor 72 may detect the corresponding reflected radar pulse 87 using the ADC 76 and the plurality of receive antennas 78-1, 78-2, 78-3 (e.g., the plurality of receive antennas are ordered in an L-shape with half wavelength distances; see the inset of fig. 2 such that the phase differences between the different antenna pairs relate to azimuth and elevation, respectively). The processor 72 may process the raw data samples obtained from the ADC 76 to a greater or lesser extent. For example, a measurement frame (sometimes also referred to as a data frame or a physical frame) may be determined and output.

Radar measurements may be implemented as a Fundamental Modulated Continuous Wave (FMCW) principle. Frequency chirping may be used to implement radar pulse 86. The frequency of the chirp can be tuned in the frequency range of 57GHz to 64 GHz. The transmitted signal is backscattered with a time delay corresponding to the distance of the reflective object captured by all three receiving antennas. The received signal is then mixed with the transmitted signal and then low pass filtered to obtain an intermediate signal. The frequency of the signal is significantly lower than the frequency of the transmitted signal and thus the sampling rate of the ADC 76 may be reduced accordingly. The ADC may operate at a sampling frequency of 2MHz and 12 bits accuracy.

As shown, scene 80 includes a plurality of objects 81-83.

Each of these objects 81-83 has a certain distance to the antennas 78-1, 78-2, 78-3 and moves at a certain relative speed with respect to the sensor 70. These physical quantities define the range and doppler frequency of the radar measurement.

For example, objects 81-83 may relate to three people; for a demographics application, the task would be to determine that the scene includes three people. In another example, objects 81, 82 may correspond to the background, while object 83 may relate to the user's hand—thus, object 83 may be referred to as a target or target object. Based on the radar measurements, gestures performed by the hand may be identified. For ease of illustration, some gestures are shown in fig. 3.

Fig. 3 schematically shows such gestures 501-510 of gesture class 520 and corresponding labels 115, but other gestures are also possible. According to the techniques described herein, gestures 501-510 may be reliably and accurately classified. More generally, according to various examples disclosed herein, classification predictions may be reliably and accurately made.

Typically, the classification predictions are based on one or more observable quantities captured in the input data provided to the ML algorithm. Some observable quantities are described in connection with fig. 4.

Fig. 4 schematically shows aspects concerning two observable quantities 108, 109 characterizing a certain gesture class, here a "circular motion" gesture, i.e. a rotating finger motion.

Illustrated is a one-dimensional time series 101. The time series 101 indicates the distance 108 of the object. Also shown is a time series 102 of doppler shifts 109 (or simply doppler frequencies) indicative of the subject.

FIG. 5 schematically illustrates a processing pipeline for implementing gesture classification. Such processing may be implemented, for example, by processor 62 upon loading program code from memory 63.

As shown in fig. 5, the classification ML algorithm 111 obtains the input feature vector 101. The input eigenvectors encode the corresponding observables of the radar measurement. Thus, the input feature vector corresponds to a representation of the radar measurement dataset. The input feature vector 101 may, for example, correspond to a row-by-row representation of RDI.

The ML algorithm 11 then proceeds to sort prediction 115, for example, to indicate a particular gesture class or to indicate the number of people.

Fig. 6 is a flow chart of a method according to various examples. The method may be performed by at least one processor, for example, when program code is loaded from memory. For example, the method of fig. 6 may be performed by processor 72 and/or processor 62 (see fig. 1 and 2).

Further, different blocks at fig. 6 may be performed by different processing devices.

The method of fig. 6 involves the operation and maintenance of the classification algorithm 111.

At block 3005, a training phase of classification algorithm 111 is implemented. Here, among other tasks, values of a plurality of parameters of the classification algorithm 111 are set, i.e., training is performed. The weight of NN may be adjusted.

The training may be based on one or more penalty values defined by the respective penalty function. The penalty value penalty may be determined based on the difference between the NN's predictions of training feature vectors for the training data set in its current training state and the corresponding benchmark truth labels of the training data set.

Iterative optimization can be achieved. Here, multiple sets may be used to adjust weights in multiple iterations. Each iteration may include a back propagation training algorithm for adjusting weights from the output layer of the NN toward the input layer.

Once the training of block 3005 is complete, an inference phase may be implemented at block 3010. Here, the classification prediction is performed without a reference truth tag available. The weights of the NN determined in the training at block 3005 are used.

Based on the inference at block 3010, one or more applications may be implemented. For example, the HMI may be controlled. HMI may be used to control a machine. Access control may be provided.

As indicated by the dashed arrow in fig. 6, another iteration of the training of block 3005 may be performed after the inference at block 3010.

Specifically, once additional training data sets become available, the ML algorithm may be retrained. For example, once additional training data sets become available, the ML algorithm may be retrained by joint learning. Here, the deployed sensor may provide training feature vectors of previously invisible scenes, such that a reference truth label may be generated.

In some scenarios, any retraining may be jointly performed in subsequent iterations of block 3005 based on one or more training data sets that have been previously used for training in previous iterations of block 3005, and one or more additional training data sets that have only become available in new iterations of block 3005. In other words, joint retraining based on previously available training data sets and new available training data sets is possible (details about such joint training will be disclosed in further detail in connection with fig. 14). For example, joint training based on an initial training data set and a joint training data set is possible. Alternatively or additionally, joint training based on the initial training data set and the enhanced training data set would be possible.

Such a technique is based on the following findings: that is, where retraining is performed based only on the new available training data set (i.e., without consideration of any initial data set), there is a risk that the overall accuracy of the ML algorithm does not increase or even decrease. In the case where retraining is performed based only on the new set of available training data, there is a risk of how the ML algorithm forgets to solve the previous task. Thus, by such joint retraining, overall accuracy may be improved.

Fig. 7 is a flow chart of a method according to various examples.

The method of fig. 7 may be performed by a processing device. For example, the method of fig. 7 may be performed by the processing device 60. The method of fig. 7 may be performed by a cloud server. For example, the method of FIG. 7 may be performed by processor 62 when loading program code from memory 63 and when executing program code.

The method of fig. 7 involves training an ML algorithm, such as ML algorithm 111 (see fig. 5). Thus, the method of fig. 7 may implement block 3005.

The ML algorithm performs classification prediction based on the radar measurement dataset. For example, the ML algorithm may make classification predictions, such as demographics or gesture classification, based on RDI or 2-D angle graphs.

At block 3105, a training data set is acquired. The training data set includes training feature vectors and associated reference truth labels. In other words, the training data set includes training feature vector pairs in the reference truth labels. The reference truth label specifies the expected output of the ML algorithm.

For example, the training data set may be loaded from memory. The training data set may be obtained from a database.

The benchmark truth labels may be annotated beforehand by an expert. The reference truth labels may be determined based on alternative measurement techniques, e.g., camera-based monitoring of training scenarios, etc. The training data set may be generated by simulation.

Next, at block 3110, weighting factors are determined for the training feature vectors; that is, each training feature vector is assigned an associated weighting factor. The weighting factors specify the impact of a particular pair of training feature vectors and reference truth labels on the training of the ML algorithm. For example, a larger (smaller) weighting factor may amplify (suppress) the effect of a corresponding pair of training feature vectors and reference truth labels on the adjustment of the parameters/weights of the ML algorithm due to the corresponding pair of training feature vectors and reference truth labels.

The weighting factors are determined using XAI analysis of the ML algorithm in its current training state.

As a general rule, XAI analysis can provide meta-information about the performance of the ML algorithm. Different training states of the ML algorithm result in different meta-information.

XAI analysis of various options is available. For example, xia Puli (shape) values may be determined. Shapley provides the additive effect of each feature on a particular local prediction of the ML algorithm. See, for example, lundberg, scott m and "A unified approach to interpreting model predictions" of Su In Lee (Advances In neural information processing systems (2017)) -the so-called SHAP method is an approximation of Shapley. Other options may also be used, see "Why should I trust you" by Ribeiro, marco Tulio, samer Singh and Carlos guestin? "Explaining the predictions of any classifier" (Proceedings of the 22nd ACM SIGKDD international conference on knowledge discovery and data mining.2016) -the so-called LIME method. In addition, other techniques are disclosed herein, "Grad-cam++" Generalized gradient-based visual explanations for deep convolutional networks "(2018 IEEE winter conference on applications of computer vision (WACV). IEEE, 2018) by Chattopadhay, aditya et al.

Then, next, at block 3115, training of the ML algorithm may be performed, i.e., the weights may be adjusted. Training is performed based on a penalty value determined based on a difference between a respective classification prediction performed by the ML algorithm for each of a plurality of training feature vectors of the training dataset acquired at block 3105 in a current training state and a reference truth label of the training dataset. Here, the penalty value is obtained by weighting such differences using a respective weighting factor associated with each training feature vector.

Next, details regarding the determination of the weighting factor at block 3110 will be disclosed. Various options may be used to determine the weighting factors at block 3110 and some options will be disclosed.

For example, for a given input data, XAI analysis can quantify the reliability of predictions made by ML algorithms in their current training state. For example, if for a given training feature vector XAI analysis yields low prediction reliability of the ML algorithm in its current training state, a large weight may be assigned to that training feature vector; on the other hand, if for a given training feature vector the XAI analysis yields a large predictive reliability of the ML algorithm in its current training state, then a small weight may be assigned to that training feature vector.

In another scenario, individual contributions to predictions made by the ML algorithm associated with individual feature values included in the training feature vectors may be considered. Thus, the determining of the weighting factor for each of the plurality of training feature vectors of the training data set may comprise: for each training feature vector of the plurality of training feature vectors, an associated feature correlation vector is determined using XAI analysis. The feature correlation vector may include feature correlation values that indicate contributions of feature values of the respective training feature vectors to the classification predictions made by the ML algorithm in the current training state.

Such feature correlation values may be determined for different classification predictions. Typically, the classification predictions output by the ML algorithm will include probabilities for different classes. Thus, one of the candidate classes is represented as the most probable class (with the highest probability). The benchmark truth tag specifies one of the candidate classes as the observed true class. The real class may be different from the most probable class or the same as the most probable class.

In general, XAI analysis can output an associated feature correlation vector for each of the candidate classes. According to an example, the weighting factor may be determined based on feature correlation vectors associated with training feature vectors, and the weighting factor may be determined for the most likely class of ML algorithm in the current training state. These feature correlation vectors may specify the relative contribution of each feature value of the associated training feature vector to the prediction of the most likely class by the ML algorithm (i.e., which feature values have a positive or negative and/or high or low impact on the prediction of the most likely class of ML algorithm) by the feature correlation values.

There are different options for considering the feature correlation vector. In a first option, the absolute value of the maximum or minimum feature correlation value of each feature correlation vector may be considered, and then the weighting factor is determined based on the absolute value. In general, the absolute value of the maximum or minimum feature correlation value indicates a strong local contribution of the feature value of the training feature vector to the prediction made by the ML algorithm. A large absolute value in the feature correlation vector indicates a "hot spot" in the contribution to the prediction. In case the classification task is strongly influenced by the individual feature values, a relatively large weighting factor may be assigned to the respective training feature vector. In a second option, the variance of the feature correlation values included in the feature correlation vector may be considered. For example, some eigenvalues may have a negative contribution to the predictions made by the ML algorithm, while other eigenvalues have a positive contribution to the predictions made by the ML algorithm; this results in a variance between the correlation values of the feature correlation vector. The larger the variance of the feature correlation values, the larger the corresponding weights. In particular, the variance of the feature correlation vector may be considered as an indicator of the complexity of the classification task. This facilitates assigning more weight to the training of such complex classification tasks.

A third option for determining weights based on feature correlation vectors is shown in fig. 8. Thus, the techniques associated with fig. 8 may be used as part of block 3110.

Fig. 8 schematically illustrates a processing pipeline for determining weights 650 associated with training feature vectors 610. The training feature vector 610 includes a plurality of feature values 611, 612, 613 (in the example shown, the training feature vector 610 is 3-dimensional, but may generally have any dimension). For example, training feature vector 610 may represent RDI.

The training feature vectors 610 are processed in the XAI analysis 119. For example, a Shapley value may be determined. In particular, feature correlation vectors 630, 640 may be determined. The feature correlation vector 630 is associated with the most probable class (i.e., the class with the highest probability of all candidate classes) predicted by the ML algorithm 111. On the other hand, feature correlation vector 640 is associated with reference truth label 615 (i.e., the true class). The feature correlation vector 630 includes feature correlation values 631, 632, 633; and feature correlation vector 640 includes feature correlation vectors 641, 642, 643.

For example, the feature relevance value 631 indicates the predicted marginal contribution of the feature value 611 to the ML algorithm 111 corresponding to the most likely class. The feature correlation value 641 indicates the predicted marginal contribution of the feature value 611 to the ML algorithm 111 corresponding to the real class. Similarly, a correlation value 632 is associated with a feature value 612, and a correlation value 642 is associated with the feature value 612. Correlation value 633 is associated with feature value 613; and a correlation value 643 is associated with the feature value 613.

In the example shown in fig. 8, the weighting factors 650 associated with training feature vector 610 are then determined based on the combination 659 of feature correlation vector 630 and feature correlation vector 640.

Various options may be used to implement the combination 659. For example, the absolute value of the mean subtraction (or vice versa) of the feature correlation vector 630 from the feature correlation vector 640 may be determined:

wherein M is 1 Representing feature correlation vectors 630, M 2 Represents feature correlation vector 640, and M 1i And M 2j Representing the corresponding correlation value. N is a dimension (3-D (3-dimension) in the illustrated example).

The absolute value of the IoU combination of feature correlation vectors 630, 640 ("the combination of the cross ratios (Intersection over Union)") may also be determined.

Such a technique provides the advantage of taking into account the deviation between the nominal protection of the real class and the actual prediction of the most likely class at the feature level. Thus, training feature vectors that show significant deviations in the relative contribution of individual feature values to the predictions of the (wrong) most likely class compared to the predictions of the real class may be weighted more significantly in training.

Next, aspects related to performing training with weighting factors in mind are disclosed in connection with fig. 9.

Fig. 9 schematically shows a processing pipeline for performing training. Thus, fig. 9 may be used to implement block 3115. As shown in fig. 9, ML 111 provides predictions (i.e., most probable class 115) based on training feature vectors 610. At 691, the most likely class 115 is compared to the benchmark truth label 615. Based on the comparison, a loss value is calculated based on the corresponding loss function. At 692, the penalty value may be weighted using the weight 650, and the weighted penalty value 690 may then be used to adjust the weight of the ML algorithm 111. For example, back propagation may be used to achieve gradient descent optimization.

Fig. 10 is a flow chart of a method according to various examples. The method of fig. 10 may be performed by a processing device. For example, the method of fig. 10 may be performed by the processing device 60. For example, the method of FIG. 10 may be performed by processor 62 when loading program code from memory 63 and when executing program code. The method of fig. 10 involves training an ML algorithm, such as ML algorithm 111 (see fig. 5). The ML algorithm performs classification prediction based on the radar measurement dataset. For example, the ML algorithm may make classification predictions based on RDI or 2-D angle graphs, such as demographics or gesture classification.

The method of fig. 10 may be combined with the method of fig. 7.

Initially, at block 3205, a training dataset is acquired. Block 3205 corresponds to block 3105.

At block 3210, an enhanced training data set may be determined based on a plurality of training feature vectors included in the training data set. The enhanced training data set includes one or more enhanced training feature vectors.

The enhanced training dataset may be determined by applying at least one data transformation associated with a physical observable associated with the radar measurement dataset to the training feature vector.

Then, at block 3215, training of the ML algorithm is performed. In particular, training may be performed based on both the training data set acquired at block 3205 and the enhanced training data set acquired at block 3210. Joint training is possible.

The training performed at block 3215 corresponds to the training performed at block 3115.

Additional training data is made available by determining an enhanced training data set. This helps to improve the overall accuracy of the ML algorithm in making classification predictions. By applying the data transformation to the training feature vectors, new training feature vectors may be obtained for enhancing the training data set. Because the data transformation is associated with the physical observables associated with the radar measurement data set, the input vector space of feature vectors input to the ML algorithm may be oversampled. The data transformation corresponds to an offset of the position in the input vector space.

According to some examples, the reference truth label may be unchanged relative to the data transformation. This means that the reference truth labels are not affected by the data transformation. The additional reference truth labels of the enhanced training data set may then correspond to the reference truth labels of the training data set. An example data transformation is shown in fig. 11. The left side of fig. 11 shows training feature vectors, here specifically RDI 811, of the initial training data set acquired at block 3205. The right side of FIG. 11 shows the enhanced training feature vectors of the enhanced training data set derived from RDI 811, here specifically corresponding RDI 812, acquired at block 3210. The data transformation includes a frequency flip 871 (vertical axis in fig. 11) of doppler observables. For some prediction tasks, such frequency roll-overs 871 of the Doppler observables do not affect the prediction class, i.e., the benchmark truth labels will be unchanged. One example is detecting finger rotational movement (see fig. 4) -if clockwise or counterclockwise movement is not distinguished. On the other hand, if the clockwise and counterclockwise movement of the finger are distinguished, then the frequency flip 871 of the Doppler observables will affect the reference truth label (change from clockwise to counterclockwise movement or vice versa). Another example data transformation is shown in fig. 12. The joint training of the ML algorithm 111 is achieved by alternately providing the ML algorithm 111 in the respective training state with the training feature vectors as input, and the weights of the ML algorithm 111 are updated accordingly (e.g., as explained above in connection with fig. 9). Sequence 680 may define such alternate training based on different training feature vectors.

In summary, techniques have been disclosed that facilitate accurate training of ML algorithms for classification tasks, taking into account XAI analysis.

In addition to more accurate training of the ML algorithm, the disclosed techniques may also improve transparency by creating human-understandable reasons for decisions of the ML algorithm. Examples of antagonism may be disclosed. Furthermore, by increasing the confidence in the decisions, trust in predictions made by the ML algorithm can be increased.

Techniques have been disclosed to explain why ML algorithms provide mispredictions. This is based on and accounts for multiple artificial intelligence analyses. Based on such XAI analysis, the robustness of the ML algorithm can be improved by retraining.

Furthermore, enhancement techniques for enhancing training data sets have been disclosed. A data transformation associated with the physical observables may be applied to the training feature vectors to obtain enhanced training feature vectors. Examples include frequency flipping along the doppler dimension, shifting along the range dimension, and so forth. Furthermore, since the radar measurement dataset is sensitive to noise, gaussian noise may be added to the training feature vector. This facilitates the implementation of the ML algorithm in a particularly robust manner.

To counteract catastrophic forgetfulness, progressive learning may be employed. After each reasoning step, a joint retraining based on both the initial training data set and the new available training data set is possible each time a new training data set is available.
